title: Authentication works locally but fails behind a reverse proxy
description: Problem: Authentication works locally but fails behind a reverse proxy. Solve this problem with multiple approaches and detailed explanations.

data.text: A Next.js application authenticates users perfectly on localhost, but after deploying behind Nginx or a cloud load balancer, users are immediately redirected back to the sign-in page or receive token errors. The application itself did not change; the network path did. This is a classic environment-boundary bug.
Why it works locally but breaks in production

items: Cookies set on localhost are accepted without a domain, but production cookies need an exact domain or secure flag.
Reverse proxies terminate TLS and forward requests over HTTP, stripping or changing headers the app relies on.
NextAuth v5 trusts the X-Forwarded-Proto and Host headers only when explicitly configured.
The auth callback URL registered with the identity provider must match the production origin exactly.
Session tokens stored in httpOnly cookies may be rejected if SameSite or Secure attributes are mismatched.
CORS and CSRF protection behave differently when the frontend and API are served from different origins.

terms.definition: A server that sits in front of a web application and forwards client requests, often handling TLS termination, load balancing, and caching.
A proxy whose headers the application is configured to accept, because the proxy is under your control.
A cookie attribute that controls when the browser sends the cookie with cross-site requests, used to mitigate CSRF.
A cookie attribute that restricts transmission to HTTPS only. Browsers reject Secure cookies over plain HTTP.

data.text: Inspect the Network tab in production DevTools. Look at the auth callback request and response headers. If the Set-Cookie header is missing, or if the cookie is present but not sent on the next request, the problem is almost always cookie configuration, trust proxy settings, or a mismatched callback URL.

data.title: Do not trust all proxies blindly
data.text: Enabling trustHost globally in a multi-tenant environment can allow header spoofing. Only trust proxies that terminate TLS in front of your application, and prefer explicit allow-lists over catch-all flags.

cards.description: Required when the frontend and auth API are on different origins.

data.caption: Authentication flow behind a reverse proxy
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[User visits https://app.example.com] --> B[Reverse proxy terminates TLS]
    B --> C[Proxy forwards request with X-Forwarded-Proto: https]
    C --> D[Next.js app receives request]
    D --> E{trustHost enabled?}
    E -->|Yes| F[App trusts Host and X-Forwarded-Proto]
    E -->|No| G[App treats request as HTTP and rejects secure cookies]
    F --> H[Auth cookie is set with Secure flag]
    G --> I[Auth callback fails or redirect loop]
    H --> J[User session persists across requests]
    I --> K[User sees sign-in page repeatedly]

items.question: Why does the callback URL need to match exactly?
items.answer: OAuth providers compare the callback URL registered in the developer console with the one sent in the authorization request. A mismatch causes the provider to reject the request before issuing a code.

items.question: Should I use AUTH_TRUST_HOST or trustHost?
items.answer: In NextAuth v5, trustHost tells the framework to trust the Host and X-Forwarded headers. Use it when you control the proxy and know it terminates TLS correctly.

items.question: How do I debug cookie issues?
items.answer: Check the Application tab in DevTools: look at the cookie domain, path, Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite attributes. Also check the Network tab for the Set-Cookie header on the auth callback response.

data.title: Reproduce and fix a proxy auth failure
data.description: Set up a local reverse proxy in front of a Next.js app and break auth, then fix it.
steps: Create a minimal Next.js app with NextAuth Google OAuth.
Start the app on port 3000 and set up Caddy or Nginx on port 443.
Visit the proxy URL and attempt to sign in.
Compare cookie behavior with and without trustHost enabled.
Fix the configuration so auth works through the proxy.
data.expectedOutcome: You should be able to explain which header or cookie attribute changed between localhost and the proxy, and you should have a working production-like auth flow.

data.title: Summary
points: Reverse proxies terminate TLS and can strip or rewrite headers.
NextAuth v5 requires trustHost when behind a proxy so it reads X-Forwarded headers.
OAuth callback URLs must match the production origin exactly.
Cookie attributes like Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite must align with the deployment topology.
Debug with DevTools Application and Network tabs before changing code
data.takeaway: Authentication bugs at the proxy boundary are infrastructure problems masquerading as application bugs. Trace the request from the browser through the proxy to the app to find the mismatch.
